CI is only passing when the value is enabled. clang-tidy failures are present with disabled but they disappear with enabled value (see diff between patchset 3 and 4, CI passed for patchset 4 but failed for 3). My assumption is that with disabled, clang-tidy is not able to find compilation-database for the files added in this patch.

> We'd enable in out meta layer.

That's generally not how this repo works.  All features are enabled by default (and features should operate properly when enabled and not have impact unless enabled in EM config), platforms can disable them if they like for space savings.

As `ocp_ami_pack_header`, `ocp_ami_encode_reason_code` and `ocp_ami_decode_reason_code_and_cc` all return ocp_ami_completion_codes, is there any specific reason why the return type is `uint8_t` here and not `int`? (or vice-versa, not `uint8_t` for other two functions)
Been over a week.  Comments still not addressed.

I had originally given this feedback in private, but was asked by multiple people to give it publicly to give it visibility, so here it goes.

This patchset is going about things backwards.  We don't add a new folder, THEN come up with an application that uses it.  We develop an application with the basics (meson support, EM support, etc) THEN we start adding features to it.  If we then have some distinct data structures that might be useful outside the project, we add them the "simple" way the first time (per the developing guide)

This commit series also goes deep into the "We should have a C library" that has already been discussed at TOF level, and rejected for the moment, given we don't even have the basic use cases working and no code had been pushed.  Lets get the basic path working, then if we want to refactor out some C/C++ libraries, we can do that on patchset N.  The initial series of patches should get temperatures reading properly.

If you want a library, that's fine, we (NV) can pull out the relevant headers and make our library, but for the moment there's just a bunch of VDM commands that don't go in a library called "OCP".  There are two structs defined in OCP, the code should match that.

Continuing, we shouldn't be inventing our own clang tidy.  If we don't pass the one that's there, lets discuss further why that is, and which checks need bypassed.


To summarize:
Patchset 1: Add GPU management daemon
Patchset 2: Add EM config reading support to dbus-sensors
Patchset 3: Add EM support to em repo
Patchset 4: Add GB200 EM config
Patchset 5: Implement basic temperature reading in C++ using a minimum implementation.
Patchset 6: Test on gb200-nvl72 target and verify function

After those patches are pushed, we will be in much better shape I think.

boost asio class for datagram socket boost::asio::local::datagram_protocol::socket uses AF_UNIX as the socket domain. And we need to use AF_MCTP as the socket domain. Based on my reading of the boost asio documentation there is no way to specify the socket domain for the class boost::asio::local::datagram_protocol::socket.
Why are we setting peek here?  Can't we just read the message directly?

With these flags we would read the length of the received message and allocate the buffer for that size. And in the subsequent recvfrom call, we would read the message into that buffer. This pattern to read the received messages is referenced from the pldm stack.
sockFd is only used in this method.  It does not need to be at class scope.
Please use the overload of assign that does not throw an exception.  It compiles smaller and in this case (where we're just returning) would result in less code.
sockFd is used in other methods of the class.
Per the coding standard, no lambdas over a few lines.  Please make a normal method.
I asked this above, but why are we doing recvfrom here with peek?  Can we not just read the message?

With MSG_PEEK flag, we would read the length of the received message and allocate the buffer for that size. And in this recvfrom call, we would read the message into that buffer. This pattern to read the received messages is referenced from the pldm stack.

The intent was that because this does implement a spec that in theory could evolve, and AMD has an implementation of (even if it requires lots of VDM) we could keep it generic.  FWIW, We did the same thing with Intel originally, calling it cpu-sensor, then later changed to intel-cpu-sensor when it was clear that AMD/ARM/Other CPUs wouldn't be able to reuse most of the code.
